title: The Collector's Vault
subtitle: Data Wrangling Assignment · group_by + summarise
story: You are a forest ecologist on an alien world — and, if you’re honest, an avid collector that might spend more time on their collections than on their ecology. Your days are spent high in the canopy, riding the cable cars between research stations, measuring impossibly tall trees and cataloguing what you find. But every evening ends the same way: you make the long climb to the cliff, and attempt to open the sealed alien gate you have never once managed to unlock. They say a true artifact waits inside. Today you’ll make your rounds one more time — and try the vault again.

done.title: The way is clear!
done.body: You read the grove census the careful way, and the boulder rolls aside. Golden hour spills over the last stretch of trail — the cliff, and the vault, are just ahead.

escapeDone.title: The vault opens!
escapeDone.body: Three shapes, three groupings — you matched every line’s collection to how it was sorted, and the ancient gate finally swings wide. Inside, at last, the artifact. It’s yours. The mist lifts over the canopy as the sun goes down.

musicCredit.text: Yuuf - In The Sun (Live in Surrey Hills)

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster of a lone alien cliff-side vault gate glowing with a single warm amber light at sunset, set into a rocky mountain precipice above an endless sea of misty tree canopy. Designed to read clearly as a small thumbnail: one bold, simple, high-contrast silhouette, iconic and uncluttered, minimal fine detail. Flat, limited palette: deep teal, icy blue, and one warm amber glow. Soft film grain, painterly but clean with simple geometric shapes. Strong negative space, single centred focal subject. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from a large research platform DEEP in the shadowy lower reaches of a colossal alien tree — the lowest and deepest station of the climb, ground and sky both hidden, mist rising from below and sinking from above, immense dark trunks vanishing into the haze all around, only a few faint rays of light filtering down through the gloom. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is an open, unbroken stretch of sky and distant horizon: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, immense alien tree-trunks close and enclosing, rising up into drifting mist above and plunging down into drifting mist below — the deep shadowy view that wraps unbroken around behind you; to the left, hanging lanterns of amber lichen strung along the living-wood railing, a warm point of light in the gloom; left of centre, a weathered field card pinned to the living-wood railing; dead ahead in the centre, a weathered field instrument of brass and timber with an open console screen showing a faint bar chart, its pale glow one of the few points of light in the dark; just right of centre, oversized softly-glowing fungal shelves clustered on a dark living-wood trunk, bioluminescent in the gloom; to the right, a small alien monorail gondola docked at the platform edge, boarded directly through its own sliding door — a bold square motif on the door — the gondola's cables rising straight up and vanishing into the dark misty trunks overhead; on the far right, more immense dark trunks and drifting mist above and below, matching the view on the far left where they meet cleanly at the seam directly behind you. Deep, dim and mysterious but never sinister; cool teal-blue shadow and heavy drifting mist both above and below, pierced by only a few faint god-rays, with the warm amber glow of lichen-lanterns and drifting bioluminescent spores the only points of warmth; painterly, cinematic, subtle film grain — the darkest, most enclosed scene of the whole climb. No people, no lettering, no text, no captions, no UI; no mountains, no open sky or distant vista, no bright sunshine. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into an open, unbroken stretch of sky and distant horizon, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

hotspots.body:
A note on your pinned up record:
The gleam-beetles again — I can never work a transect without pocketing a few. No two the same: some no bigger than a seed, some broad as a thumbnail, and every one throws the canopy-light back a little differently. Back home I lay them out and just look at them for a while. There's an order in a good collection, if you sit with it long enough.

hotspots.label: The bark-calipers

check.prompt: The long distance bark calipers have logged the trunk girth of every tree in the grove. Considering all the trees of each species together, which species grows the widest around on average? Assign that species' name to answer.
check.hint: Group the trees by species and take the mean trunk_girth_cm of each.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: Bloomspire grows the widest around, ~36 cm mean girth.
wrong: Group by species and summarise the mean girth: forest_census |> group_by(species) |> summarise(m = mean(trunk_girth_cm)).
The widest kind is the group with the largest mean — arrange(desc(m)) and read the top row's species.
You want the single widest species on average — not the widest individual tree, and not the commonest kind.

Field-note, tucked under a rock.
Rank the groves by the vigour of whatever's standing in them and the same grove keeps winning. But that grove is thick with the hardy kinds — trees that read strong wherever they root. check.prompt: Here, the question is not which grove happens to hold the strongest trees (highest vitality index), but which ground truly grows a tree best — giving every kind of tree an equal say, whatever grows there. Which grove is the finest ground to grow in? Assign its name to answer.
check.hint: A raw grove average is swayed by which species happen to grow there. Give every species an equal say first.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted: giving every species an equal say, Sunspire Heights is the finest ground to grow in (~64) — the quick tally's answer was a mirage.
wrong: First take each species' mean vitality WITHIN each grove: group_by(grove, species) |> summarise(m = mean(vitality_index)).
Then average those per-species figures up to the grove, so no common species dominates: group_by(grove) |> summarise(mm = mean(m)) |> arrange(desc(mm)).
If you land on the same grove the quick tally gave, the common species are still voting twice — balance by species first.

rooms.debrief: The boulder asked the same question as the third station — which ground truly grows a tree best? — but demanded the honest answer. Group by grove and species first, summarise, then ungroup and regroup by grove alone, and the winner flips from Cragside to Sunspire Heights. The shortcut's grand mean had been dragged around by whichever species happened to crowd each grove; balancing the species first is what a fair comparison of grounds actually takes. That regroup was the capstone the whole ladder was built to earn.

rooms.title: The cliff-top vault

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the windswept cliff-top at the very highest point, at sunset, the mist wholly lifted to reveal a full vista of the alien canopy and the far ridge of peaks — an ancient alien gate set into the rock face, a blank three-by-three button panel beside it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the open sunset sky over the vast distant sea of alien tree-canopy and the far ridge of peaks — one unbroken, glowing band of gold, rose and teal cloud meeting the faraway horizon: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the trail leading back down off the cliff-top toward the boss ledge and the cars below; to the left, the full sunset vista off the cliff — the whole alien canopy and a far ridge of peaks glowing under drifting sunset cloud, the mist entirely gone; left of centre, carved alien runes ringing the great stone gate, faintly bioluminescent in the fading light; dead ahead in the centre, the ancient alien gate set into the cliff face, and beside it a blank three-by-three grid of unlit stone buttons awaiting the correct pattern; to the right, hanging lanterns of amber lichen strung along a weathered rail at the cliff edge, swaying in the wind. Painterly, cinematic, awe-struck and triumphant; rich sunset light — gold, rose and deep teal — over a vast clear vista, gentle bioluminescent amber and rune-glow, subtle film grain; the payoff moment, warm and wondrous. No people, no lettering, no text, no captions, no UI. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the open sunset sky over the vast distant sea of alien tree-canopy and the far ridge of peaks — one unbroken, glowing band of gold, rose and teal cloud meeting the faraway horizon, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

rooms.debrief: No console, no code — just the gate and what you'd already seen. Three shapes down the columns, three traits across the rows, and one press per line to say how its car was sorted: □ colour, ○ size, △ shape. That is group_by with the labels stripped off — recognising which grouping produced a pile you were handed, instead of computing it. Match all three and the ancient gate swings wide: the skill you'd been coding all day, made into a lock.

worldPlatePrompt: This is a panorama. A sweeping 360-degree establishing view of an alien forest-canopy world: colossal alien trees with living-wood research platforms and railings, weathered brass-and-timber instruments, hanging lanterns of amber lichen strung along the rails, drifting bioluminescent spores in the air, and a monorail of small cable-cars running between the treetops. The misty canopy falls away into hidden depths below, and a distant ridge of pale mountain peaks breaks through the golden haze. Painterly, cinematic, cheerful and hopeful; the teal-and-amber house palette — warm gold light with soft teal shadows, gentle bioluminescent glow — in soft, even daylight (deliberately neither dawn nor sunset, so each room can set its own time of day). Subtle film grain. No people, no lettering, no text, no captions, no UI.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: The whole day's round was one skill wearing a forest for a costume: group_by + summarise — sort many things into piles by a shared trait, then read one number off each pile. Every station binned the census a different way and read one summary from it; every cable car was a collection someone had already sorted, waiting only to be recognised; and the vault opened when you matched each line to the trait it was grouped by. Here is how each part embodied the wrangling.
